BEYOND THE WASTE

Lagos is buried in its own waste.

Refuse is dumped in marketplaces, beside roads and along drains across Lagos. Our documentary shows how these heaps block movement, disrupt trade and make daily life harder for millions of people.

What is the crisis?

Lagos produces more waste every day than its collection system can carry away. Refuse, garbage and rubbish end up in markets, on roadsides, under bridges and in drains all over the city.

In the markets the problem is easy to see. Waste piles up between stalls, on walkways and beside the places where people sell food and clothes. Our photos show mounds of discarded clothing, shoes, plastic bags, sachets and bottles, with traders and passers-by working right beside them.

The markets we visited, Oshodi among them, are only one part of a city-wide crisis. What happens there shows how a fast-growing city struggles to keep up with its waste, and how that disrupts the way people live and work.

13,000+ tonnesof waste generated in Lagos every day, according to the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA)
30–50%of Lagos' waste is formally collected, according to one recent assessment. The rest is dumped, burned or left on the street
Under 10%of Lagos' plastic waste is recycled, according to the Lagos State Government

How waste disrupts daily life

Lagos runs on movement: people walking to work, buses on the road, traders opening stalls, goods arriving. Uncollected waste gets in the way of all of it.

Movement and transport

Heaps spill onto walkways and roads, forcing pedestrians into traffic and slowing buses and vehicles. Commutes take longer and become less safe.

Trade and income

Traders lose customers when stalls sit beside rotting rubbish. Goods get dirty, shoppers stay away, and a market that should earn money loses it.

Drains and flooding

Waste blocks drains and canals, so rain water cannot flow away. Roads, shops and homes flood, and work stops until the water goes down.

Health and time

Sickness from dirty air, water and food means missed days of work and school, plus money spent on treatment, for families and traders alike.

Air: smoke, smell and dust

Rotting rubbish gives off a strong smell and gases such as methane. When heaps are set on fire to reduce them, the smoke carries fine particles that are easy to breathe deep into the lungs. Passing vehicles also stir up dust from dried waste.

What this means for Lagos

  • Traders, commuters and residents near dumps breathe the smoke and smell all day
  • Smoke from burning plastic contains harmful chemicals
  • Methane from rotting waste adds to climate change

Water: blocked drains and flooding

Plastic bags, bottles and sachets get washed or pushed into drains and canals. They block the flow of water, so when it rains the water backs up and spreads onto roads and into stalls and homes.

What this means for Lagos

  • Blocked drains cause flooding after heavy rain
  • Floodwater carries dirt and germs from the rubbish into markets, streets and homes
  • Liquid from rotting waste can seep into the ground and nearby water

Soil and food

Across Lagos, food is sold and eaten close to waste heaps. Flies, rats and cockroaches feed on the rubbish and then land on food, while dirty water and dust settle on goods on display. Plastic does not rot, so it stays in the ground for a very long time.

What this means for Lagos

  • Food near rubbish can be contaminated by pests and dirty water
  • Plastic in the soil breaks into tiny pieces that remain for years
  • Waste left in the open spoils markets and streets and hurts business

Health effects

Piles of rubbish and standing water create ideal places for mosquitoes, flies and rats to breed. Children, older people and people with breathing problems are most at risk, as well as the traders and waste workers who are exposed every day.

What this means for Lagos

  • Diseases such as cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea spread through dirty water and food
  • Stagnant water in blocked drains lets malaria mosquitoes breed
  • Cuts from broken glass and metal, and breathing problems from smoke, affect workers

What can be done

Traders and shoppers

Keep stalls and streets tidy, use bins, never dump in drains or on roadsides, and separate plastic, paper and food waste where possible.

Market leaders

Agree on clear dumping points and regular clean-up times for every market, and work with licensed waste collectors so refuse is removed daily.

Government and LAWMA

Provide enough bins and trucks, clear drains before the rainy season, and enforce rules against illegal dumping and open burning.

Recycling and reuse

Plastics, cardboard and old clothes have value. Collection points and recyclers can turn market waste into income.
